title: Testing a Next.js App
summary: Test a Next.js app at every level: Vitest for components and server code, MSW for the API, and Playwright against a production build.
intro: A Next.js app runs in two places, the browser and your server, and its bugs hide in both: a form that shows the wrong error, an action that forgets to check the session, a page that never streams in its cart count. The React course gave you the tools: Vitest and Testing Library for components, MSW for the network, and Playwright for whole journeys. This lesson fits them to Next.js. You'll see which tool tests which piece, set up Vitest for client and server code, test a Server Action as a plain function, run Playwright against a production build, learn why `page.route` can't reach the server's own requests and what to do instead, and finish with visual tests and a CI run.

steps.title: What to test, and with which tool
steps.body:
The React course sorted tests into levels: unit, integration, and end to end, with fast narrow tests at the bottom and slow realistic ones at the top. Next.js adds a twist. Some of your code runs only on the server, some runs in both places, and some, like an async Server Component, can't be rendered by a unit test runner at all yet. Choosing the level by where the code runs saves you from fighting your tools.

## Three kinds of code, three ways to test

```diagram testing-nextjs-levels
Pick the tool by where the code runs, and push logic down to the faster rows.
```

The top row is code that doesn't need Next.js to run: Client Components, hooks, and pure functions, like a price formatter or a zod schema. **Vitest** renders them in **jsdom**, a pretend browser that runs inside Node.js, and Testing Library clicks and types the way a person would. A test takes milliseconds.

The middle row is server code that's a plain async function: Server Actions, the server-only modules in `lib/`, and the helpers they use. A Vitest test can import and call them in Node.js, with Next.js's request functions, like `cookies()`, swapped for fakes, and the network answered by MSW.

The bottom row is everything that only exists once Next.js is running: async Server Components, layouts, routing, streaming with Suspense, `proxy.ts`, caching, and an action's round trip. **Playwright** tests those in a real browser, against the app built the way it ships.

## Why not render async Server Components in Vitest?

The Next.js docs say it plainly: Vitest doesn't support async Server Components yet, so test them end to end. React's test renderer expects a component to hand back its JSX straight away, and an async component hands back a promise. Even with a workaround, the test would skip what matters most about such a component: the data cached with `use cache`, the Suspense boundaries that stream, and the cookies of a real request.

So keep Server Components thin. Let them read data and lay it out, and move the logic into pieces you can test quickly: the data module, the action, a pure helper, a Client Component. What's left in the page gets one end-to-end test that loads it and checks the pieces are wired together. A Server Component that isn't async and doesn't read the request is just a function that returns JSX, so it renders in Vitest like any other.

## Actions are just functions

The lesson on Server Actions showed what an action is on the network: a POST with an ID in a header. In a test, none of that exists. `createReview` is an exported async function that takes a slug, the previous state, and a `FormData`, and returns a state. You import it and call it. That makes actions some of the easiest code in the app to test thoroughly, including the cases a browser test would take seconds each to reach: a missing title, a `409` from the API, or a visitor who isn't logged in.

The same design helps the Client Components. The review form gets its action as a prop, so a test can pass a fake function and decide exactly what it returns, as the example shows. The form doesn't know or care that the real one runs on a server.

## How many of each

Most of your tests should be the fast kinds, as the testing trophy in the React course said, with integration tests the widest band. For a Next.js app that means many Vitest tests for components and actions, and a handful of Playwright journeys: log in, review a product, check out. Add one end-to-end test for each page that streams, redirects, or depends on `proxy.ts`, since those only happen with Next.js running.

examples.title: A Client Component with a fake action
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/review-form.test.tsx`: the review form from the Server Actions lesson, tested with a fake action and no server.
examples.explanation: `ReviewForm` is the Client Component from the Server Actions lesson, which wraps its `action` prop in `useActionState`. Here the action is `vi.fn()`, a fake that answers with field errors the first time and a message the second, the same shapes the real `createReview` returns. The test picks a rating and presses Post review, the way a person would, then waits with `findByText` for the error to appear. It types a title, presses again, and waits for the message. Last, it reads the `FormData` the form sent on the second call, since `useActionState` passes the previous state first and the form data second. No server, no Next.js, and no network are involved, so the test runs in about a tenth of a second.

steps.title: Vitest in a Next.js project
steps.body:
Vitest knows nothing about Next.js. It doesn't read `next.config.ts`, it doesn't know that `@/` means the project's root folder, and it has never met the App Router that `next/navigation`'s hooks expect to find around them. A few lines of setup fix all three, and one comment per file decides whether a test runs like a browser or like your server.

## Install it

```bash
npm install -D vitest @vitejs/plugin-react jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/dom @testing-library/user-event @testing-library/jest-dom @types/node@24
```

Vitest 5 needs Node.js 22.12 or newer, and it wants the Node.js type definitions to match. A project from `create-next-app` has `@types/node` version 20, so npm refuses with an `ERESOLVE` error, its way of saying two packages want different versions of a third. Raising `@types/node` to 24, which matches the Node.js 24 you installed with Hack University, settles it. Then add `"test": "vitest"` to the scripts in `package.json`. `npm test` watches your files and runs the tests again on every save, and `npx vitest run` runs them once.

## The config file

The first example is `vitest.config.mts`, next to `package.json`. `@vitejs/plugin-react` compiles JSX, as in the React course. `resolve.tsconfigPaths: true` makes Vite 8 read the `paths` in `tsconfig.json`, so `@/lib/api` resolves in tests the way it does in Next.js. The Next.js docs use the `vite-tsconfig-paths` plugin for the same job, which older Vite versions need. `environment: "jsdom"` makes jsdom the default, and the setup file adds jest-dom's matchers, like `toBeInTheDocument`, and cleans the page after each test. The `exclude` keeps out the `e2e` folder, which belongs to Playwright.

## Faking the router

A Client Component that calls `usePathname` or `useRouter` expects the App Router around it, and a test has none. Without a fake, they fail in two different ways. `usePathname()` returns `null`, so the `NavLink` in the second example crashed with Cannot read properties of null (reading 'startsWith'). `useRouter()` throws invariant expected app router to be mounted.

The fix is `vi.mock("next/navigation", ...)`, which swaps the whole module for one you write, before the component imports it. The second example replaces `usePathname` with `vi.fn()`, then each test sets what it returns with `vi.mocked(usePathname).mockReturnValue(...)`. For `useRouter`, return an object with `push`, `replace`, `back`, and `refresh` as `vi.fn()`, and check afterwards that `push` was called with the right path.

## Server code runs in node

jsdom fills the test's world with browser things, like `window` and `document`. Server code should run where it really runs, in plain Node.js, so a file of server tests starts with this comment as its first line:

```ts sketch
// @vitest-environment node
```

That file then runs without jsdom, and MSW's `setupServer` catches the requests Node.js makes, which the next part uses.

## server-only in a test

The data modules from earlier lessons start with `import "server-only"`, which turns importing them into a client file into a build error. In a test, that guard fires too. The third example imported the review action, whose `lib/api.ts` imports `server-only`, and the whole file failed before a single test ran.

The package works by having two versions. Its normal one throws an error. Its other one, picked under the `react-server` condition that Next.js uses when it builds server code, is an empty file. Vitest picks the normal one. So server tests replace it with an empty module, one line at the top of the file:

```ts sketch
vi.mock("server-only", () => ({}));
```

That's safe, since the build still enforces the guard where it matters: in your real client code.

examples.title: The config and the setup file
examples.prompt: `vitest.config.mts` and `vitest.setup.ts`, both in the project's root folder, shown together.
examples.explanation: The top half is `vitest.config.mts`. `include` finds every file ending in `.test.ts` or `.test.tsx`, wherever it sits, so a test can live next to the file it tests, like `review-form.test.tsx` beside `review-form.tsx`. The bottom half is `vitest.setup.ts`, which Vitest runs before each test file. Importing `@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest` adds the DOM matchers to `expect`. `cleanup` removes whatever a test rendered, so the next test starts from an empty page. Testing Library does that by itself only when Vitest's functions are global, and this config keeps them imported instead, which is clearer to read.

examples.title: Mocking next/navigation
examples.prompt: `components/nav-link.test.tsx`: testing a link that marks the current section, with `usePathname` faked.
examples.explanation: `NavLink`, in `components/nav-link.tsx`, is a Client Component that wraps `Link` and sets `aria-current="page"` when the current path is its `href` or starts with it, so screen readers announce which section you're in. Vitest moves `vi.mock` calls to the top of the file, above the imports, so the component gets the fake module. `usePathname` is now a `vi.fn()`, and `vi.mocked` tells TypeScript that, so `mockReturnValue` type-checks. Each test pretends to be on a different page and checks the attribute. `Link` itself needs no fake: outside the App Router it renders a plain `a` element.

The line under it points at `node_modules/server-only/index.js`, which tells you the guard fired and not your code.

steps.title: Testing Server Actions as functions
steps.body:
A Server Action holds the rules that matter most in your app: what counts as a valid review, who may post one, and what happens when the API says no. Those rules deserve fast tests that cover every branch. Since an action is an async function, a test can call it with a real `FormData` and check what it returns, as long as the test supplies the three things Next.js normally provides: the request's cookies, the cache functions, and an API to talk to.

## Fake what Next.js provides

`createReview`, from the Server Actions lesson, reads the session cookie through `apiFetch`, which calls `cookies()` from `next/headers`, expires the cached reviews with `updateTag` from `next/cache`, and may call `redirect` from `next/navigation`. Outside a request, the first two throw. `cookies()` says `cookies` was called outside a request scope, and `updateTag` says it can only be called from within a Server Action. So the test replaces them with `vi.mock`:

- `next/headers` becomes an object whose `cookies()` returns a fake cookie store, with a `get` that hands back a session token.
- `next/cache` becomes `{ updateTag: vi.fn() }`, so the test can check which tag the action expired.
- `server-only` becomes an empty module, as the previous part explained.

`redirect` stays real. It works outside Next.js, because all it does is throw.

## Catch the redirect

`redirect("/login?next=...")` throws an error whose `message` is `NEXT_REDIRECT`, and whose `digest`, a property Next.js reads to know what to do, holds the details: `NEXT_REDIRECT;replace;/login?next=/products/trail-pack-45;307;`. That's the kind of redirect, the path, and the status code, separated by semicolons. A test checks both: that the call rejects with `NEXT_REDIRECT`, and that the digest names the right path. Next.js keeps its own `isRedirectError` helper internal, so match on the digest rather than importing it.

## Answer the API with MSW

The action calls the Trailhead API through `apiFetch`, which reads the base URL from `process.env.API_URL`. Vitest doesn't load your `.env` files into `process.env`, so the test sets it with `vi.stubEnv("API_URL", "http://api.test/v1")`, a made-up address no real server answers. Then MSW, from the React course, answers it. `setupServer` from `msw/node` catches every request Node.js makes, and each test adds the handlers it needs with `server.use`.

Start the server with `server.listen({ onUnhandledFrame: "error" })`. That's MSW 3's name for the option MSW 2 called `onUnhandledRequest`, and with `"error"`, a request no handler answers fails the test, saying which request it was. Without it, an action could quietly reach a real network. After each test, `server.resetHandlers()` drops the handlers that test added, so the next one starts clean.

A handler can also check what the action sent. The second test in the example records the `Cookie` header and the JSON body, then checks that the session was forwarded as `th_session=token-1`, and that the rating arrived as the number 4, not the string from the form.

If your project generates code from Trailhead's OpenAPI spec with Kubb, as in the React course, its MSW plugin gives you a handler for each operation, and you can pass those to `setupServer` in place of handwritten ones.

## What the four tests cover

The example covers each branch of `createReview`: bad input is turned away without calling the API, good input is posted with the session and expires `reviews-trail-pack-45`, a `401` turns into a redirect to the login page, and a slug that isn't a slug throws before any request is made. The run in the second example finishes in under a second, along with the component tests from the earlier parts.

examples.title: Every branch of createReview
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/actions.test.ts`: the review action called with real FormData, with Next.js's functions faked and the API answered by MSW.
examples.explanation: The three `vi.mock` calls replace what Next.js would provide, and Vitest moves them above the imports so `createReview` gets the fakes. `beforeAll` and `afterAll` start and stop MSW once for the file, and `afterEach` resets both the handlers and the mocks' records of their calls. `reviewForm` builds a `FormData` the way a submitted form would, and each form has a short review body, since the action requires one, so only the field a test is about can fail. The first test never adds a handler, so if the action called the API anyway, MSW's `"error"` setting would fail the test. The third test stores the promise in `result` and checks it twice, once for the message and once for the digest. The last one passes `../me`, the path trick from the Server Actions lesson, and expects the slug check to throw.

steps.title: Playwright against a production build

examples.title: The Playwright config
examples.prompt: `playwright.config.ts` in the project's root folder: the Trailhead API and a production build as web servers, and a setup project for logging in.
examples.explanation: `testDir` keeps Playwright's tests in `e2e/`, away from Vitest's. In CI, `forbidOnly` fails the run if someone left a `test.only` behind, `retries` tries a failed test twice more, the `github` reporter marks failures on the pull request, and the `html` reporter writes a report you can open later. On your computer, `list` prints one line per test. `trace: "on-first-retry"` records a trace, the step-by-step recording from the React course, when a test fails and runs again. The two projects run `setup` first, then everything else with Sam's saved cookies. `timeout: 180_000` gives the build three minutes, since `next build` takes much longer than starting a dev server. The first server is the Trailhead API, started from its folder next to the project, and `TRAILHEAD_TEST: "1"` turns on the reset that the setup project calls.

examples.title: A journey and a static shell
examples.prompt: Two tests from `e2e/`, using Sam's saved session: posting a review, and checking what arrives before the stream.
examples.explanation: Two journeys from `e2e/`. The first is the whole review flow: the form, the Server Action, the API, `updateTag`, and the list rendered again, all real. It checks the message, then finds the new list item and checks it's by Sam, which proves the saved session reached the action. The second checks the static shell. Inside `instant()`, the page loads with the product's name and the Suspense fallback, Checking your cart..., and no cart count at all. Once the callback ends, the held-back stream is let through, and the last line waits for the real count. `baseURL` is passed in because `instant()` sets a cookie for the site before the first page loads, and needs to know which site.

steps.title: Mocking the server's own requests
steps.body:
In the React course's app, every API request came from the browser, so `page.route` could catch any of them and answer with whatever the test wanted: an empty list, a `500`, a slow reply. A Next.js app moves most of those requests to the server. The browser asks for a page, and the server fetches the data. That changes what a test can intercept, and it's the most common surprise when you bring Playwright to Next.js.

## page.route sees only the browser

`page.route` works inside the browser Playwright controls. It sees every request that browser sends: pages, scripts, images, the RSC payloads of navigations, and Server Action calls. It never sees a request that your Next.js server sends to the API, since that one goes from one server to another, and the browser isn't part of it.

```diagram testing-nextjs-server-fetch
page.route sits in front of the browser. The server's fetch goes around it.
```

The browser asks for `/products/...`, and `page.route` could answer that. Then the server, rendering the page, fetches `/v1/cart` from the API on its own. That's the request a test usually wants to control, and it's out of reach.

The first example proves it. The test tells `page.route` to answer every request for `/v1/cart` with a cart holding 99 items, and records each request it catches. Then it opens a product page. The run in the second example shows the page with `In your cart: 0`, the real empty cart from the API, and `page.route` caught 0 requests: the cart was fetched by the server, and the browser never asked for it.

## Point the server at an API you control

The reliable fix is to decide where the server's requests go before the app starts. Your server code reads the API's address from `API_URL`, so the test run sets it to an API it controls. That's what the `webServer` list in the previous part does: it starts the Trailhead API, then builds and starts the app with `API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1`. Every fetch the server makes goes there.

The Trailhead API serves fixed seed data from memory, and puts it back on `POST /__reset`. An API made only for tests can go further and let a test change its answers, through an endpoint of its own, like one that makes the next cart request fail. The Trailhead API has no such endpoint, which leaves test mode, below, for a test like that. MSW's `setupServer` can't take this job from inside a test file: it catches requests made in the process that runs it, and the server's fetches happen in the Next.js process, not in Playwright's. That's why the course runs the Trailhead API as a server of its own, which the app reaches over the network like any real API.

Build the app with the API's address, not just start it with it. Values read while prerendering are baked into the static pages at build time, which is why the config sets `API_URL` on the command that runs both `next build` and `next start`.

## Next.js test mode, experimental

Next.js ships an experimental way to answer the server's fetches from inside a test, called **test mode**. Turn on `experimental.testProxy` in `next.config.ts`, again only for the test build, and import `test` and `expect` from `next/experimental/testmode/playwright` instead of `@playwright/test`. Each test gets a `next` fixture, and `next.onFetch` sees every `fetch` your server makes while rendering that test's pages. Return a `Response` to answer it, `"continue"` to let it through to the real address, or `"abort"` to fail it. A fetch no handler answers is aborted.

It works by having Playwright add headers to every browser request, which tell the server where the test is listening. The server then sends each of its own fetches there first. The third example ran and passed on a cart page. Be careful with it, though. It's experimental, so its name and behavior can change in any release, and in our tries with Next.js 16.4 and Cache Components, turning it on broke the product page, whose data is cached with `use cache`, with a prerendering error. Treat it as a tool for a few special tests, and keep an API you start for the run, like the Trailhead API, as your default.

examples.title: A route the server goes around
examples.prompt: `e2e/server-fetch.spec.ts`: a test that tries to answer the cart request with `page.route`, and counts what it catches.
examples.explanation: `page.route("**/v1/cart", ...)` catches any request whose URL ends in `/v1/cart`, whatever the host, and `route.fulfill({ json })` would answer it with that JSON and never let it reach the network. The handler also pushes each URL it catches into `seen`. The product page's `CartCount` is an async Server Component inside Suspense that fetches the cart through `apiFetch`, so the test waits for the count to appear, prints what the page shows and how many requests were caught, and checks that the list is empty. This test exists to teach the point. In your own suite, `page.route` stays useful for what the browser really fetches, like images or a third-party script.

examples.title: What page.route caught
examples.output:
Running 2 tests using 1 worker

  ✓  1 [setup] › e2e/auth.setup.ts:3:6 › log in as Sam (274ms)
page shows: In your cart: 0
page.route caught: 0 requests
  ✓  2 [chromium] › e2e/server-fetch.spec.ts:3:5 › page.route never sees the server's fetch to the API (125ms)

  2 passed (5.0s)
examples.explanation: Naming one file runs only its tests, plus `setup`, which the `chromium` project depends on. The two printed lines are the evidence. The page says `In your cart: 0`, which is Sam's real, empty cart from the Trailhead API, not the 99 the route would have answered with. And the route caught no requests at all, because the browser never asked for the cart. The server fetched it while rendering, and put the count in the HTML it streamed. If you see a test like this fail in your own app, with the route catching a request, that data is being fetched in the browser, by a Client Component.

examples.title: Answering a server fetch in test mode
examples.prompt: `e2e/testmode.spec.ts`, using Next.js's experimental test mode to answer the server's cart fetch.
examples.explanation: This test needs a build with `experimental.testProxy: true`. `next.onFetch` registers a handler for the fetches the server makes while rendering this test's pages. It gets a standard `Request`, so the handler reads its URL. For the cart, it returns a `Response` built with `Response.json`, holding seven items, and for anything else it returns `"continue"`, which lets the fetch through to the real address. The page at `/cart` renders `CartCount` inside Suspense, and the count shows 7, a number that exists only in the test. That's something `page.route` couldn't do. It passed on this page, which has no `use cache` data, and the same setup broke the cached product page.

steps.title: Visual tests and CI
steps.body:
Two kinds of bugs slip past everything so far. A change to a shared style can push a button off the page while every test still finds it by role and clicks it. And tests that only run on your computer catch nothing when a teammate forgets to run them. Visual tests cover the first, and CI, continuous integration, the service that runs your checks on every push, covers the second.

## Screenshots with the moving parts masked

`await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot("product-page.png")`, from the React course, takes a screenshot and compares it with a saved one, pixel by pixel. The first run has nothing to compare with, so it fails with A snapshot doesn't exist, writing actual, and saves the picture next to the test, in `e2e/visual.spec.ts-snapshots/`. Look at it, commit it, and from then on every run compares against it.

A Next.js page mixes a static shell with parts that stream in per visitor, and those parts change from run to run: a cart count, a date, the newest reviews. Wait for them to arrive, so the page has settled, then hide them with `mask`, which paints each matching element a solid color before comparing. The first example masks the cart count. Playwright turns off animations while it takes the screenshot, so a moving element doesn't fail the comparison.

## One machine for screenshots

The saved file was named `product-page-chromium-darwin.png`. The `darwin` is macOS: Playwright adds the operating system to the name, because the same page draws differently on different systems. Fonts are drawn with slightly different edges, and a missing font is replaced by another one. On the Linux machine CI runs on, Playwright looks for `product-page-chromium-linux.png` instead, and even a picture made on another Linux computer can differ if its fonts do.

The fix is to take every screenshot on the same machine. Microsoft publishes a Docker image with Playwright, its browsers, and their fonts, tagged with the Playwright version, and both you and CI run the visual tests inside it:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/work -v /work/node_modules -w /work mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.64.1-noble sh -c "npm ci && npx playwright test e2e/visual.spec.ts --update-snapshots"
```

Docker, from the deployment lesson, runs a program inside a container, a sealed-off Linux system with exactly the files its image holds, so it behaves the same on every computer. `-v "$PWD":/work` shares your project folder with it. `-v /work/node_modules` gives the container a `node_modules` folder of its own, since `npm ci` inside it installs Linux versions of packages that your Mac or Windows copy can't use. `--update-snapshots` saves new pictures in place of the old ones, which is the command to run when a change to the page is on purpose. Pick the image tag that matches your `@playwright/test` version exactly. Keep visual tests to a few key pages, since each picture is one more thing to update when the design changes.

## Unit tests first, then end to end

The second example is a workflow for GitHub Actions, the CI service built into GitHub, saved as `.github/workflows/test.yml`, that runs on every push and pull request. It runs in two jobs. `unit` installs and runs Vitest, which takes seconds. `e2e` waits for it with `needs: unit`, so a broken action fails the run in under a minute, without waiting for a build. `e2e` runs inside the Playwright image, so the browsers are already there and the screenshots match the ones you saved with Docker.

`next build` keeps a cache in `.next/cache`: compiled code, and the data it fetched while prerendering. Without it, every CI build starts from nothing, and Next.js warns that no cache was found. The `actions/cache` step saves that folder at the end of the job and restores it at the start of the next, keyed on the lockfile and the source files. The Next.js docs give that exact key. On a failure, the `upload-artifact` step keeps the HTML report, traces included, so you can download it from the run's page and see what the browser saw.

examples.explanation: `e2e/visual.spec.ts` first waits for the streamed cart count, so the screenshot is of a finished page. `fullPage: true` takes the whole page, not only the part in the window. `mask` takes locators, and each element they match is painted over in magenta in both pictures before they're compared, so the count can be any number. The output is the second run, `npx playwright test e2e/visual.spec.ts`, after the first had saved the picture. The comparison passed. Change the page's spacing or a font, and it fails, with the expected picture, the new one, and a third that marks the pixels that differ.

examples.title: A CI workflow
examples.prompt: `.github/workflows/test.yml`: Vitest first, then Playwright in its Docker image, with the Next.js build cache kept between runs.
examples.code:
name: test
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx vitest run

  e2e:
    needs: unit
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.64.1-noble
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: .next/cache
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-nextjs-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}-${{ hashFiles('**/*.ts', '**/*.tsx') }}
          restore-keys: ${{ runner.os }}-nextjs-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}-
      - run: npx playwright test
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report
examples.explanation: `on` runs the workflow for every push and pull request. Each job gets a fresh Linux machine, and `npm ci` installs exactly what the lockfile says. In `e2e`, `container` runs every step inside the Playwright image, and `CI` is set, so the config starts both servers fresh, retries failures twice, and uses the `github` reporter. The cache `key` changes whenever the lockfile or a source file changes, so a new entry is saved. `restore-keys` lets a run whose source changed still start from the newest cache made with the same packages, since most of it is still good. This file was written for the lesson and not run here, since it runs on GitHub's machines. That's the end of the path the first lesson mapped out: a Next.js app you can build, ship, and test.

recap:
- Test Client Components and pure code with Vitest in jsdom, server code in the node environment, and async Server Components end to end.
- Vitest needs plugin-react, tsconfig paths, and mocks for next/navigation, and server tests replace server-only with an empty module.
- A Server Action is a function: call it with FormData, fake cookies() and updateTag, catch NEXT_REDIRECT, and answer the API with MSW.
- Run Playwright against next build and next start, with a setup project that saves a logged-in storageState.
- page.route only sees the browser, so point API_URL at an API the test run starts, like the Trailhead API, and keep Next.js test mode for special cases.
- Mask the streamed parts in screenshots, take them in one Docker image, and run unit tests before end-to-end tests in CI with .next/cache kept.
